topics.name: Courts, Sources of Law & Erie Basics
terms: Concurrent jurisdiction
Both state and federal courts may hear the same type of case, so the plaintiff chooses.
Exclusive federal jurisdiction
Congress has allowed only federal courts to hear a type of case.
Article III, Section 2
The constitutional list of the kinds of cases federal courts may hear.
Rules Enabling Act
28 U.S.C. § 2072, letting the Supreme Court write procedural rules that cannot alter substantive rights.
Subject matter jurisdiction
A court’s power to hear the type of dispute at issue; it can’t be waived or conferred by consent.
Court of limited jurisdiction
A court that may hear only the categories of cases authorized to it, like a federal district court.
Certiorari
The Supreme Court’s discretionary review of a lower court decision.
Civil action
The single kind of lawsuit under Rule 2, which merged the old separate systems of law and equity.
Erie doctrine
In diversity cases, federal courts apply state substantive law and federal procedure.
Federal general common law
Judge-made law that federal courts applied under Swift v. Tyson until Erie rejected it.
Rules of Decision Act
28 U.S.C. § 1652, which Erie read to require federal courts to apply state law where federal law doesn’t govern.
Choice of law rules
Rules a court uses to decide which state’s substantive law governs a claim.
Forum shopping
Choosing a court in hopes of getting a more favorable rule.
Predictive approach
Where state law is unclear, a federal court asks what the state’s highest court would hold today.
Federal specific common law
Federal judge-made rules that survive Erie where strong federal interests require a federal rule.
cases: Swift v. Tyson
Federal courts in diversity cases could apply their own general common law.
Erie R.R. v. Tompkins
Federal courts in diversity cases must apply state substantive law.
Klaxon Co. v. Stentor
A federal diversity court applies the choice of law rules of the state where it sits.
mcq: Where are most American lawsuits litigated?
State courts
Federal district courts
The Supreme Court
Federal courts of appeals
State trial courts of general jurisdiction handle the great majority of cases (Ch. 1).
Federal courts’ subject matter jurisdiction is:
Limited to the categories Article III allows and Congress grants
Unlimited, like a state court of general jurisdiction
Limited to cases where the United States itself is a party to the suit
Whatever the parties agree to in a forum clause
Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction (Ch. 1).
Who bears the burden of showing a federal court has subject matter jurisdiction?
The party invoking federal jurisdiction
The defendant, in every case
The party opposing federal jurisdiction
The court, which must disprove it on its own
The party seeking a federal forum must establish jurisdiction (Ch. 1).
Under the Rules Enabling Act, a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure may not:
Abridge, enlarge, or modify a substantive right
Set time limits for filing papers
Regulate the scope of discovery
Govern how the summons and complaint must be served on a defendant
Can parties consent to federal subject matter jurisdiction that doesn’t otherwise exist?
No
Yes, if both sign a written stipulation
Yes, if the defendant doesn’t object in its answer
Yes, but only in diversity cases
Subject matter jurisdiction can’t be created by consent or waiver (Ch. 1).
What did Erie overrule?
Swift v. Tyson
Klaxon
The Rules Enabling Act
Article III
Erie rejected federal general common law (Ch. 24).
Under Erie, a federal court hearing a state-law claim in diversity applies:
State substantive law and federal procedure
Federal common law on every issue
State law for everything
Federal substantive law and state procedure
That is the core Erie principle (Ch. 24).
A main policy concern behind Erie was:
Forum shopping and unequal treatment of litigants
Overcrowding of state court dockets
Bias of state juries against parties from other states and countries
Delay in federal appellate review
Swift let outcomes turn on which court system was chosen (Ch. 24).
Under Klaxon, a federal diversity court picks which state’s law applies by using:
The choice of law rules of the forum state
Federal choice of law rules made by courts
The choice of law rules of the plaintiff’s home
The rules of the state where the claim arose
Klaxon extends Erie to choice of law (Ch. 24).
If a state’s highest court hasn’t clearly decided an issue, a federal diversity court should:
Predict how that court would rule today
Apply federal law
Dismiss the case
Follow the most recent trial court opinion
The state supreme court predictive approach (Ch. 24).
After Erie, does any federal common law remain?
Yes, in narrow areas with strong federal interests
No, Erie abolished all judge-made federal law
Yes, but only in diversity cases
Yes, in any case the federal judge chooses
Erie ended general, not specific, federal common law (Ch. 24).
Rule 1 says the Federal Rules should be applied to secure:
The just, speedy, and inexpensive end of every action
The fullest possible trial of every disputed fact
Uniform results matching state court practice
Encouraging parties to settle before discovery
Fed. R. Civ. P. 1.
Which court is usually a court of general jurisdiction?
A state trial court
A federal district court
A federal bankruptcy court
A federal court of appeals
State trial courts can hear most kinds of cases; federal courts are limited to what Article III and Congress allow.
Under Swift v. Tyson, federal diversity courts could disregard:
State court decisions on general common law
State statutes on any subject
The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure
State constitutional provisions
Swift read “laws” in the Rules of Decision Act to mean statutes and local law, not general common law. Erie rejected that reading.
Erie read the Rules of Decision Act’s “laws of the several states” to include:
State court decisions as well as statutes
Only state statutes, as Swift had held
Only state constitutions and statutes
Federal common law on general questions
Erie held that state law includes the decisions of a state’s highest court, not just its legislature’s statutes.
How are the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure made?
The Supreme Court promulgates them, subject to congressional review
Congress passes each rule as a statute
Each district court writes its own
The Judicial Conference adopts them with no further review
Under § 2072, the Supreme Court prescribes rules after an advisory process, and they take effect unless Congress acts.
Can the U.S. Supreme Court review a state supreme court’s decision?
Yes, on questions of federal law
Yes, on any question of state or federal law
No, state courts are fully independent
Only if the parties are from different states
The Supreme Court’s review of state decisions reaches federal questions; the state’s high court has the last word on its own law.
hypo: Ana sues Ben in federal court on a claim governed by state law. Their state’s supreme court has a rule on point, but the federal judge thinks a different rule is wiser. What should the judge do?
Follow the rule the state’s high court adopted
Follow the rule she thinks is wiser
Apply a general federal common law rule, since it’s a federal court
Apply the majority rule among other states instead
After Erie, federal courts in diversity must follow state substantive law (Ch. 24).

A diversity case is filed in federal court in State A. The claim has ties to States A and B. State A’s courts would use a choice of law rule pointing to State B’s law. Which law should the federal court apply?
State B’s law, because State A’s courts would choose it
State A’s law, because a federal court always applies the forum’s own law
Federal law, because it’s a federal court
The law of the state where the defendant lives
Klaxon: use the forum state’s choice of law rules (Ch. 24).
A federal judge in a diversity case finds a 1950 state supreme court decision on point. Strong signals suggest that court would reject the rule today. What approach does the judge use?
Predict how that court would rule now, departing only on strong evidence
Follow the 1950 decision until that court itself overrules it, however weak it looks
Apply the rule that most other states now follow
Dismiss the case because the state law is unsettled
The predictive approach, applied cautiously (Ch. 24).
Two companies want to litigate a dispute in federal court. Neither diversity nor a federal question exists. They sign a stipulation consenting to federal jurisdiction. Result?
The court still lacks subject matter jurisdiction
Jurisdiction exists by consent
Jurisdiction exists if the stipulation is filed before the answer
Jurisdiction exists if the amount exceeds $75,000
Subject matter jurisdiction can’t be conferred by agreement (Ch. 1).
A plaintiff could file her case in either state or federal court. She picks state court. Which concept describes her choice?
Concurrent jurisdiction
Exclusive federal jurisdiction
Removal
Supplemental jurisdiction
Both systems may hear the case (Ch. 1).
A proposed Federal Rule would change the elements a plaintiff must prove to win a state-law claim. What is the problem?
It would alter substantive rights, which § 2072 forbids
Only Congress can write any procedural rule
Federal Rules never apply in diversity cases, so it would be pointless
Rules can’t govern what plaintiffs must plead
§ 2072(b) limits the rules to procedure (Ch. 1).
Under Swift v. Tyson, a federal judge in a diversity case ignores a state court’s common law rule and applies her own view of the general law. After Erie, is that allowed?
No, she must apply the state rule
Yes, if the issue is commercial
Yes, if the parties agree
Only in admiralty cases
Erie: there is no federal general common law (Ch. 24).
Ana sues Ben in federal court under a federal statute. Their state’s courts follow a different rule than the statute does. Which governs Ana’s federal claim?
The federal statute
The state rule, because Erie requires state law
Whichever rule is more favorable to Ana
The state rule, unless the parties agree otherwise
Erie concerns state-law claims. When federal law creates the claim, federal law governs it.
A diversity case is filed in federal court in State C. Plaintiff lives in State D, whose courts would apply D’s law. State C’s courts would apply State E’s law. Which law applies?
State E’s law
State D’s law, the plaintiff’s home
State C’s own substantive law
Federal choice of law rules
Klaxon: the federal court uses the forum state’s (C’s) choice of law rules, which point to E.
Rae loses in her state’s supreme court on a pure question of state law. Can the U.S. Supreme Court review that ruling?
No, the state court has the final word on state law
Yes, by certiorari on any issue it decided
Yes, if she is from a different state than the other party
Yes, if the amount at stake exceeds $75,000
The Supreme Court reviews state decisions only on federal questions.
Rae loses in her state’s supreme court on her claim that a state statute violates the U.S. Constitution. Can the U.S. Supreme Court review that ruling?
Yes, it presents a federal question
No, state supreme courts have the final word in their cases
No, she needed to start in federal court
Only if the parties are diverse
A federal constitutional question decided by a state court is within the Supreme Court’s appellate reach.
Before Erie, a company reincorporated in another state just to create diversity and get a federal court to apply “general law” instead of the state’s rule. What problem did Erie target?
Forum shopping between state and federal courts
Corporations changing their state of incorporation
States refusing to honor federal judgments
Federal judges refusing state-law cases
Erie aimed to stop outcomes from turning on whether a case was in state or federal court.
A suit concerns the United States’ rights on checks it issued. No federal statute addresses the issue. What law governs?
Federal common law
The forum state’s law, under Erie
The law of the state where the check was cashed
None; the court must dismiss
Uniquely federal interests, like the government’s own financial obligations, can be governed by federal common law after Erie.
Leo files a claim under a federal civil rights statute in state court. Congress hasn’t made federal jurisdiction over it exclusive. May the state court hear it?
Yes, state courts have concurrent jurisdiction
No, federal claims belong in federal court
Only if the defendant consents
Only if the parties are also diverse
State courts can hear federal claims unless Congress makes federal jurisdiction exclusive.
In a diversity case, the state’s statute of limitations would bar the claim, but federal law has no limit for this claim. Which applies?
The state statute of limitations
No limit, because the court is federal
Whichever is longer
The court may pick either
A limitations period is treated as substantive under Erie basics.
fill: Federal courts are courts of ___ jurisdiction.
They may hear only what Article III and Congress allow (Ch. 1).
Under 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b), the Federal Rules may not abridge, enlarge, or modify any ___ right.
The Rules Enabling Act limits the Rules to procedure (Ch. 1).
In Erie, the Supreme Court overruled ___ v. Tyson.
Erie rejected federal general common law (Ch. 24).
Under Klaxon, a federal diversity court applies the choice of law rules of the ___ state.
The court uses the rules of the state where it sits (Ch. 24).
Rule ___ says the Federal Rules should secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action.
The only federal court that the Constitution itself creates is the ___ Court.
Article III creates the Supreme Court and lets Congress create inferior courts.
Under Erie, a federal court hearing a state-law claim applies state ___ law.
Erie: state substantive law, federal procedure.
After Erie, federal common law survives only in areas of uniquely ___ interest.
Federal common law is limited to narrow enclaves with strong federal interests.

topics.name: Diversity Jurisdiction
terms: Complete diversity
No plaintiff may share state citizenship with any defendant.
Domicile
Where a person lives with the intent to remain indefinitely; it fixes an individual’s state citizenship.
Principal place of business
A corporation’s nerve center, where its high officers direct and control its activities.
Amount in controversy
For diversity, what’s at stake must exceed $75,000, not counting interest and costs.
Legal certainty test
A good-faith claim over $75,000 suffices unless it is legally certain the plaintiff can’t recover that much.
Aggregation
Adding claims together to meet the amount; one plaintiff may add all claims against one defendant.
Alienage jurisdiction
Federal power over suits between U.S. state citizens and citizens of a foreign country.
Time-of-filing rule
Citizenship is measured when the complaint is filed; later moves don’t matter.
Stateless person
A U.S. citizen domiciled abroad, who can’t be a party to a diversity case.
Unincorporated association
An entity like an LLC or partnership that takes the citizenship of every member.
mcq: Diversity under § 1332(a)(1) requires:
Complete diversity and more than $75,000
Minimal diversity and more than $75,000
Complete diversity and at least $75,000
Complete diversity and any amount at all
Exceeding $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs (Ch. 3).
A corporation is a citizen of:
Where incorporated and where its nerve center is
Every state where it does substantial business
Only the state where it was incorporated
The states where its shareholders live
A corporation’s principal place of business is usually:
Where its top officers direct and control it
Where it employs the largest number of its workers
Where it makes the most sales
Where it was originally founded
The nerve center test (Ch. 3).
An LLC is a citizen of:
Each state where any of its members is a citizen
Only the state where it was organized
The state of its headquarters
Its state of organization and headquarters
Unincorporated entities take their members’ citizenship (Ch. 3).
To establish a new domicile, a person needs:
Being there plus intending to stay indefinitely
Living there continuously for at least one year
Registering to vote and getting a license there
Owning a home or other real property there
Both elements are required; the old domicile continues until then (Ch. 3).
When is citizenship for diversity measured?
When the action is filed
When the events giving rise to the claim took place
At trial
At judgment
The time-of-filing rule (Ch. 3).
A U.S. citizen domiciled in France sues a Texas citizen. Diversity?
No, a U.S. citizen living abroad has no state citizenship
Yes, under alienage jurisdiction, since she lives in a foreign country
Yes, because France and Texas differ
Only if she still owns a home in a state
U.S. citizens domiciled abroad are stateless for § 1332 (Ch. 3).
Is interest on the claim counted toward the $75,000?
No, it’s excluded along with costs
Yes, it counts like any other damages
Only interest accrued before filing
Only if the claim is for a debt
A legal representative of a decedent’s estate is a citizen of:
The state where the decedent was a citizen
The state where the representative lives
The state where the estate is probated
Every state where estate property sits
Two plaintiffs each have separate $40,000 claims against one defendant. Can they combine them to meet the amount?
No, separate plaintiffs can’t add separate claims
Yes, plaintiffs who sue together may add them
Yes, if the claims arise from one event
Only if the defendant consents
Aggregation is generally allowed only for one plaintiff against one defendant (Ch. 3).
For Article III purposes, diversity requires only:
Minimal diversity
Complete diversity
Diversity plus over $75,000
Diversity among all of the plaintiffs
Article III needs just one plaintiff diverse from one defendant; § 1332 is narrower.
A partnership’s citizenship is:
That of every partner
The state of its principal place of business
The state where it was formed
That of its managing partner only
Unincorporated associations take the citizenship of all their members.
Does a claim for exactly $75,000 meet § 1332’s amount requirement?
No, it must exceed $75,000
Yes, $75,000 is the minimum
Yes, once costs are added
Only if interest is added
The amount must exceed $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.
A court dismisses for failing the amount requirement only when:
It is legally certain the plaintiff can’t recover over $75,000
The plaintiff can’t prove over $75,000 at trial
The defendant disputes the amount in its answer
The jury later awards $75,000 or less
The plaintiff’s good-faith claim controls unless it appears to a legal certainty that it can’t exceed the amount.
Which of these people is NOT a citizen of any state for diversity purposes?
A U.S. citizen domiciled in Germany
A student at college who intends to stay there
A soldier stationed abroad who is still domiciled in Ohio
An Ohio resident who vacations abroad for a year
A U.S. citizen domiciled abroad is “stateless” and can’t sue or be sued in diversity.
hypo: Pat (Ohio) sues Dee (Ohio) and Ray (Indiana) in federal court on a state-law claim for $200,000. Is there diversity jurisdiction?
No, a plaintiff and a defendant share Ohio citizenship
Yes, because one defendant is from Indiana
Yes, because the amount exceeds $75,000
Only as to the claim against the Indiana defendant
Complete diversity fails if any plaintiff shares citizenship with any defendant (Ch. 3).
Lu moves from Utah to Idaho for a two-month summer job, planning to return to Utah in the fall. She sues an Idaho citizen in July. Lu’s citizenship?
Utah, since she plans to go back
Idaho, since she lives and works there now
Both Utah and Idaho
Neither, since she is between homes
Domicile needs intent to remain indefinitely (Ch. 3).
Acme Inc. is incorporated in Delaware and its officers run the company from Chicago, Illinois. Most of its factories are in Ohio. Acme’s citizenship?
Delaware and Illinois
Delaware and Ohio
Delaware only
Delaware, Illinois, and Ohio
State of incorporation plus nerve center (Ch. 3).
When Kim files suit against a Nevada corporation, she is domiciled in Oregon. A month later she moves to Nevada permanently. Does the court still have diversity jurisdiction?
Yes, citizenship is measured when the case is filed
No, her move destroyed diversity
No, unless she moves back to Oregon before trial
Only if the defendant doesn’t object to the move
The time-of-filing rule (Ch. 3).
Jo (Idaho) sues an LLC organized in Delaware with its headquarters in Texas. One LLC member lives in Idaho. Diversity?
No, the LLC shares Idaho citizenship with Jo
Yes, the LLC is a Delaware citizen
Yes, the LLC is a Texas citizen
Yes, the LLC is a Delaware and Texas citizen
An LLC takes the citizenship of each member (Ch. 3).
Sam (Utah) sues Tia (Colorado) for $60,000 on one claim and $20,000 on an unrelated claim. Is the amount requirement met?
Yes, she may add claims against the same defendant
No, unrelated claims can’t be added together
No, each claim must exceed $75,000 alone
Only if both claims arise from one event
Aggregation is allowed here (Ch. 3).
Max (Montana) sues Lee (Wyoming) asking for $90,000, though at trial he recovers only $30,000. Did the federal court have jurisdiction?
Yes, if his $90,000 demand was made in good faith
No, the recovery fell below the amount
No, jurisdiction ends once the verdict is low
Only if Lee never objected
The legal certainty test looks at the good-faith claim at filing (Ch. 3).
A citizen of Mexico sues a California citizen for $100,000 in federal court. What basis supports jurisdiction?
Alienage jurisdiction under § 1332(a)(2)
Federal question jurisdiction under § 1331
Supplemental jurisdiction under § 1367
None; foreigners must sue in state court
Suits between state citizens and foreign citizens qualify (Ch. 3).
Pat (Ohio) sues Dee (Indiana) and Ray (Kentucky) in federal court for $200,000, claiming they jointly caused one loss. Is there diversity jurisdiction?
Yes, complete diversity and enough in controversy
No, the defendants are from different states
Yes, but only if both are served in Ohio
No, each claim must exceed $75,000 per state
Defendants needn’t share a state; what matters is that no plaintiff shares citizenship with any defendant.
Lu moves from Utah to Idaho for a new job, sells her Utah home, and plans to stay in Idaho indefinitely. Two weeks later she sues a Utah citizen. Diversity?
Yes, Lu is now an Idaho citizen
No, she hasn’t lived in Idaho for a year
No, not until she registers to vote in Idaho
No, she is between domiciles
Presence plus intent to stay indefinitely creates a new domicile immediately; no waiting period applies.
Acme, incorporated in Delaware and run from Illinois, is sued in federal court by a Delaware citizen on a state-law claim. Diversity?
No, Acme is also a Delaware citizen
Yes, the plaintiff and Acme’s headquarters differ
Yes, if most of Acme’s business is in Illinois
Yes, a corporation’s state of incorporation doesn’t count
A corporation is a citizen of both its state of incorporation and its principal place of business.
Jo (Idaho) sues an LLC organized and headquartered in Idaho. All of the LLC’s members are Oregon citizens. Diversity?
Yes, the LLC is an Oregon citizen
No, the LLC was organized in Idaho
No, the LLC is headquartered in Idaho
No, LLCs can’t be parties in diversity cases
An LLC’s citizenship comes only from its members, not where it was organized or headquartered.
Sam (Utah) sues Tia (Colorado) for $60,000 and, on a separate claim, Uma (Colorado) for $20,000. Is the amount requirement met?
No, claims against different defendants can’t be added
Yes, the total exceeds $75,000
Yes, because both defendants are Colorado citizens
Yes, if both claims appear in one complaint
A plaintiff may aggregate claims only against a single defendant (or jointly liable defendants).
Sam (Utah) sues Tia and Uma (both Colorado), claiming they are jointly liable for a single $90,000 loss. Is the amount requirement met?
Yes, the joint claim is worth $90,000
No, it must be split to $45,000 each
No, each defendant must owe over $75,000 alone
Only if both defendants consent
When defendants are jointly liable, the full joint amount counts against each.
Ines, a citizen of Spain admitted to the U.S. for permanent residence and domiciled in Florida, sues a Florida citizen in federal court for $100,000. Jurisdiction under § 1332?
No, she can’t sue a citizen of her own state of domicile
Yes, alienage jurisdiction covers any foreign citizen
Yes, if she has lived in the U.S. for over five years
Yes, alienage cases don’t require different states
§ 1332(a)(2) excludes suits between a citizen of a state and a permanent resident alien domiciled in that same state.
A citizen of Japan sues a citizen of Brazil in federal court for $500,000 on a state-law claim. Diversity or alienage jurisdiction?
No, a suit between two aliens alone doesn’t qualify
Yes, alienage jurisdiction
Yes, they are from different countries
Yes, if the suit is filed where one of them lives
Alienage jurisdiction needs a U.S. state citizen on one side; aliens on both sides alone won’t do.
Ned sues for $100,000 under a state statute that caps his kind of damages at $50,000. Does the federal court have diversity jurisdiction?
No, it is legally certain he can’t recover over $75,000
Yes, his demand controls
Yes, at least until the jury decides
No, but only if the defendant proves bad faith
A legal cap makes it legally certain the claim can’t exceed $75,000.
The day before filing suit against a Nevada corporation, Kim moves from Oregon to Nevada intending to stay. Diversity?
No, she was a Nevada citizen when she filed
Yes, she was from Oregon when the dispute arose
Yes, she hasn’t lived in Nevada long enough
Yes, because the corporation was the one that moved first
Citizenship is measured on the filing date, and a new domicile starts at once.
A corporation is incorporated in Delaware and its officers direct it from Delaware, but all its plants are in Ohio. An Ohio citizen sues it. Diversity?
Yes, it is a citizen only of Delaware
No, its operations make it an Ohio citizen
No, a corporation is a citizen wherever it works
Only if it has no Ohio employees
Hertz: the nerve center, not the plants, is the principal place of business.
An Idaho resident is appointed to represent the estate of a man who died a Utah citizen. She sues a Utah citizen for the estate. Diversity?
No, she takes the decedent’s Utah citizenship
Yes, she is an Idaho citizen
Yes, the estate is a separate citizen
Only if the estate is probated in Idaho
fill: Diversity jurisdiction requires an amount in controversy that exceeds $___, exclusive of interest and costs.
A corporation is a citizen of its state of incorporation and the state of its principal place of ___.
Under Hertz, a corporation’s principal place of business is its ___ center.
The place where high officers direct and control it (Ch. 3).
Complete diversity means no plaintiff is a citizen of the same ___ as any defendant.
Strawbridge: § 1332(a)(1) is satisfied only if no plaintiff shares state citizenship with any defendant.
An LLC takes the citizenship of each of its ___.
Unincorporated associations take their members’ citizenship (Ch. 3).
In Strawbridge v. Curtiss, the Court read the diversity statute to require ___ diversity.
Strawbridge requires that no plaintiff share citizenship with any defendant.
A domicile requires physical presence plus intent to remain ___.
The test is presence plus intent to remain indefinitely.
Adding up a plaintiff’s claims to meet the amount in controversy is called ___.
A single plaintiff may aggregate all claims against a single defendant.

topics.name: Federal Question Jurisdiction
terms: Arising under
The phrase in Article III and § 1331 describing federal question cases.
Well-pleaded complaint rule
A federal question must appear in the plaintiff’s own claim, not in a defense or the reply to one.
Creation test
A case usually arises under federal law when federal law creates the cause of action.
Embedded federal issue
A federal question inside a state-law claim that can support jurisdiction if necessary, disputed, substantial, and resolvable without upsetting the federal-state balance.
The statute giving district courts jurisdiction over civil actions arising under federal law.
The statute giving federal courts exclusive jurisdiction over patent and copyright claims.
The statute giving federal courts admiralty and maritime jurisdiction.
Saving to suitors clause
The part of § 1333 preserving state court remedies in many maritime cases.
Anticipated defense
A federal argument the plaintiff expects the other side to raise; it can’t create federal jurisdiction.
mcq: Is there an amount in controversy requirement for § 1331?
No
Yes, over $75,000
Yes, over $10,000
Only for state-law claims
Federal question cases have no amount requirement (Ch. 4).
Under the well-pleaded complaint rule, jurisdiction depends on:
The plaintiff’s own claim, not defenses
Any federal issue raised by either side
The defendant’s answer and defenses
The citizenship of the parties
Mottley (Ch. 4).
Which is broader?
Article III’s ‘arising under’ clause
§ 1331’s ‘arising under’ language
Both are exactly the same
§ 1331, because Congress expanded it
The statute is read more narrowly than the Constitution (Ch. 4).
A federal counterclaim by the defendant:
Doesn’t supply federal question jurisdiction
Supplies jurisdiction over the whole case
Requires the case to be removed
Makes federal jurisdiction exclusive
Jurisdiction turns on the plaintiff’s complaint (Ch. 4).
Patent infringement claims can be heard in:
Federal court only
State court only
Either system, at the plaintiff’s choice
Federal court, but only if over $75,000
§ 1338(a) makes jurisdiction exclusive (Ch. 4).
A state-law claim with an embedded federal issue arises under federal law only if the issue is:
Necessary, disputed, substantial, and federally resolvable
Mentioned anywhere in the plaintiff’s complaint
Raised as a defense in the defendant’s answer to the complaint
Important to both parties and to the public
The Grable test (Ch. 4).
Most federal question cases fit which test?
Federal law creates the cause of action
The defendant is a federal agency or officer
Damages exceed $75,000
The complaint mentions a federal statute
The creation test covers most cases (Ch. 4).
Admiralty jurisdiction comes from:
In a declaratory judgment action, federal question jurisdiction depends on:
Whether the anticipated coercive suit would arise under federal law
Whether the declaratory plaintiff’s complaint mentions federal law
The Declaratory Judgment Act being a federal statute
Whether the opponent’s likely defense would be federal
Courts ask whether the suit the declaration heads off would itself fall under § 1331.
Article III’s “arising under” clause reaches any case in which federal law:
Forms an ingredient of the case
Creates the cause of action
Appears in the plaintiff’s complaint
Is the only basis of the claim
Osborn read Article III broadly; § 1331 is much narrower.
A federal court must confirm its own subject matter jurisdiction:
At every stage, even if no party objects
Only when a party moves to dismiss
Only before the answer is filed
Only in diversity cases
Lack of subject matter jurisdiction can’t be waived, and the court must raise it on its own.
When federal jurisdiction over a claim is exclusive:
State courts can’t hear the claim
Federal courts may ignore venue rules
Only the Supreme Court may hear it
The plaintiff may pick either system
Exclusive jurisdiction means only federal courts may hear that type of claim.
hypo: Pia sues in federal court on a state-law claim. Her complaint adds that the defendant will probably argue a federal statute protects it, and that the statute doesn’t apply. Federal question jurisdiction?
No, a federal defense can’t support jurisdiction
Yes, the complaint mentions a federal statute
Yes, if the federal statute is important
Only if the defendant raises it later
Well-pleaded complaint rule (Ch. 4).
Raj sues his former employer in federal court under a federal statute that gives workers a right to sue. Both are citizens of the same state, and he seeks $5,000. Jurisdiction?
Yes, his claim arises under federal law
No, the parties are not diverse
No, the amount is under $75,000
Only under supplemental jurisdiction
§ 1331 has no diversity or amount requirement (Ch. 4).
A software company sues a competitor in state court for patent infringement. What should happen?
Dismissal, because federal courts hear these exclusively
The state court may hear it, since state and federal courts share these cases
The state court hears it unless the defendant objects
The state court must transfer it to federal court

topics.name: General, Tag & Consent Jurisdiction
terms: General jurisdiction
Power over any claim against a defendant, even one unrelated to its forum contacts.

The test for all-purpose jurisdiction: affiliations so continuous and systematic that the defendant is essentially rooted in the forum.

For a corporation, its place of incorporation and principal place of business; for an individual, domicile.

Power based on serving an individual while physically present in the forum.
Consent
Agreeing to a court’s jurisdiction, by agreement, conduct, or failing to object.

An agreement choosing the court where disputes between the parties will be litigated.

Losing the defense by not raising it in the first Rule 12 response.

A state law requiring out-of-state companies doing business there to register, sometimes as consent to jurisdiction.

General jurisdiction requires affiliations so continuous and systematic the corporation is essentially at home.

Doing substantial business in a state doesn’t make a corporation at home there.

Serving an individual while voluntarily present in the state supports jurisdiction.

Where it is incorporated and headquartered
Anywhere it sells a lot of products
Anywhere it has an office
Anywhere it is registered to do business

Her domicile
Anywhere she owns property

Yes, always
Only if sales exceed half its total
Only for foreign corporations

Jurisdiction based only on internet sales
Quasi in rem jurisdiction without contacts

Wherever it has a sales office
Wherever a forum resident sues it
Wherever it sells many of its products

Any filing made before trial begins
The summary judgment motion
The final pretrial conference

Yes, through its U.S. subsidiary
Only if it is served in California

Yes, Texas is Acme’s principal place of business
No, the claim arose in Oregon
No, only specific jurisdiction is possible
Only if Acme consents to Texas

The motion is timely
The court must consider it

Yes, the incident happened in Nevada
Yes, unless the plaintiff is from Idaho

No, the events happened abroad
No, only the parent can be sued
Only with specific jurisdiction

No, Acme isn’t at home in Oregon

Yes, it was in her first Rule 12 motion
No, it must be raised alone
No, 12(b)(6) must be decided first

Only if it has employees there
Mallory upheld jurisdiction based on consent through registration.

Yes, Idaho is her domicile
No, the incident occurred abroad
No, Idaho lacks specific jurisdiction
Only if she is served in Spain
An individual is subject to general jurisdiction where domiciled.

topics.name: Notice, Service & Long-Arm Statutes
terms: Summons
The court document, issued by the clerk, that tells a defendant to appear and defend.

Formal delivery of the summons and complaint to the defendant.

Leaving papers at the defendant’s dwelling with someone of suitable age and discretion who lives there.

The 90-day deadline to serve after filing, extended for good cause.

A state statute that authorizes its courts to exercise jurisdiction over nonresidents.

A long-arm statute listing specific activities that support jurisdiction.

Rule 4(k)(1)(A)

A catch-all long-arm

Sent by certified mail in every case
Published in a newspaper of record

Its outside accountant or auditor

Emailing the papers, in any case
Posting the papers at the courthouse door
Telling the defendant about the suit by phone

The plaintiff’s lawyer, on firm letterhead
The judge, after a hearing
The U.S. marshal

topics.name: Venue

Any counterclaim not arising from the same transaction or occurrence.

Improper joinder of parties, which Rule 21 says isn’t a ground for dismissing the action.

A ruling that ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing to do but execute the judgment.

Appellate consideration of legal questions with no deference to the trial court.

Purpose to cause a consequence, or knowledge that it is substantially certain to result.
Transferred intent
Applying intent toward one person or tort to the harm actually caused to another.
Offensive contact
Touching that offends a reasonable sense of personal dignity.
Apprehension
Awareness that contact is about to occur, which need not involve fear.
Single intent rule
The view that battery requires only intent to cause the contact itself.
Dual intent rule
The view that battery requires intent to contact and intent that the contact harm or offend.
Chattel
An item of tangible personal property.
Dominion
Control over property inconsistent with the owner’s rights.
Continuing trespass
An object wrongfully left on land, which remains a trespass while it stays.
Ad coelum doctrine
The old rule that land ownership extends up to the sky and down to the depths.
Forced sale
The conversion remedy requiring the defendant to pay the chattel’s full value.
cases: Garratt v. Dailey
Intent for battery includes knowing with substantial certainty that contact will result.

A wrongful kick in class was a battery, with liability for unforeseen severe consequences.
Fisher v. Carrousel Motor Hotel
Snatching a plate from a diner’s hand was an offensive contact with his person.

Swinging a hatchet at a woman in the dark was an assault though no contact occurred.
Tuberville v. Savage
Words accompanying a gesture showed no immediate threat, so there was no assault.
Picard v. Barry Pontiac
Touching a camera the plaintiff was holding was an offensive contact.
White v. Muniz
Battery required intent that the contact be harmful or offensive.
Polmatier v. Russ
An insane person who formed intent to act could be liable for battery.
Bird v. Jones
Blocking a person’s path in one direction was not false imprisonment.
State Rubbish Collectors v. Siliznoff
Emotional distress caused by outrageous threats is actionable without physical injury.
Harris v. Jones
Mocking an employee’s stutter failed for lack of severe emotional distress.
Intel v. Hamidi
Unwanted emails that did not impair computer systems were not trespass to chattels.
Moore v. Regents
No conversion claim existed for a patient’s excised cells used in research.
Dougherty v. Stepp
Entering land without consent is actionable even without damage.
Herrin v. Sutherland
Firing shotguns through the airspace over land was a trespass.
Wishnatsky v. Huey
Briefly pushing a door on an intruder was not offensive to a reasonable person.

Yes: she was substantially certain he would hit the ground
No: she intended only to startle him, not to cause any harm
No: she never touched Paul herself
Only if Paul’s injury was serious
Garratt v. Dailey: intent means purpose or substantial certainty that the contact will occur. No intent to harm is required, and contact through the ground counts.
Which element is required for assault?
Apprehension of an imminent harmful or offensive contact
Actual physical contact with the plaintiff
Fear of a harmful contact at some later, unspecified time
Words threatening violence next week
Assault protects against apprehension (not fear) of imminent contact. Future threats and, usually, words alone are not enough.
Dev throws a rock at Ana, misses, and hits Ben. Can Ben sue Dev for battery?
Yes: his intent transfers to Ben
No: he had no intent toward Ben
Only in negligence, not battery
Only if Ben saw the rock coming
Transferred intent: intent toward one person carries over to the person actually harmed.
Hal builds a fence a few feet onto his neighbor's lot, honestly and reasonably believing the strip is his. Trespass to land?
Yes: intent to enter is enough; mistake is no defense
No: his honest and reasonable mistake about the line is a defense
No: the neighbor suffered no harm
Only if he had been warned first
Trespass requires only intent to enter the land. A good-faith mistake about ownership does not excuse it.
Rae takes her neighbor's car without permission, drives it across the country, and wrecks it. Most likely claim?
Conversion, because the interference was serious
Trespass to chattels, since she meant to give it back
No tort, since she meant to return it
Battery, because the car was damaged
Conversion is a serious interference justifying a forced sale at full value. A brief, harmless use would be trespass to chattels at most.
Ellie is shut in a room. A second door is unlocked, obvious, and safe to use. False imprisonment?
No: she knew of a reasonable way out
Yes: any confinement counts, whatever exits exist
Yes, if she felt humiliated
No: nobody touched her
Confinement must be complete. A reasonable, known means of escape defeats the claim.
A hotel manager snatches a plate from a diner's hand while shouting a slur, never touching his body. Battery?
Yes: touching something closely tied to the body counts
No: his body was never touched
No: words and gestures alone can never be a battery
Only if the diner was injured
Fisher v. Carrousel Motor Hotel: snatching an object from someone's hand is an offensive contact with the person.
D brutally beats Ann in front of her teenage son, knowing he is there. Can the son sue D for IIED?
Yes: he is immediate family and was present
No: the conduct wasn’t aimed at him
No: only the direct victim can recover
Only if he was physically hurt too
Restatement § 46(2): when conduct is directed at a third person, immediate family members present at the time may recover.
With his hand on his sword, a man says: 'If it were not assize-time, I would not take such language from you.' Assault?
No: his words negated any threat of imminent contact
Yes: putting his hand on the sword is itself a threat
Yes: any threat with a weapon is assault
Only if the listener was afraid
Tuberville v. Savage: words can strip a gesture of its menace.
In White v. Muniz, a woman with Alzheimer's struck her caregiver. The Colorado court required proof that she:
Intent to contact and intent that it harm or offend
Intent to make the contact, without any intent to harm or offend
Mere carelessness in making contact
Awareness that the contact was illegal
White applied the dual intent rule. Many courts use single intent: intent to contact is enough if the contact is in fact harmful or offensive.
In Polmatier v. Russ, a man in a psychotic state shot his father-in-law. Could he be liable for battery?
Yes: an insane person can form the needed intent
No: insanity is a complete defense to intentional torts
No: he couldn’t understand his acts
Only under a negligence theory
Insane people can be liable for intentional torts if they formed the intent to act, even from delusional reasons.
A mechanic, angry at being photographed, pokes the customer's camera without touching her. Picard v. Barry Pontiac result?
Battery, since the camera was closely tied to her
No tort, since only the camera and not her body was touched
Assault, but not battery
Trespass to chattels, but not battery
Contact with something closely attached to the plaintiff, like a camera she was holding, is contact with her.
Intel v. Hamidi: a former employee sent mass emails to Intel's servers, which kept working fine. Trespass to chattels?
No: the system itself wasn’t harmed
Yes: any unwanted use is trespass
Yes: employees were distracted
No trespass, but conversion instead
California requires actual impairment of the chattel for trespass to chattels. Lost productivity from content did not count.
Moore v. Regents: doctors used a patient's removed cells to develop a lucrative cell line. Could he sue for conversion?
No: the court wouldn’t extend conversion to his cells
Yes: his cells were his property
Yes, for the full value of the cell line developed
Only for trespass to chattels
The court rejected conversion but allowed a breach of fiduciary duty / informed consent claim.
Bird v. Jones: a crowd blocks a man's way on a bridge, but he can turn back and go another way. False imprisonment?
No: blocking one direction isn’t confinement
Yes: any obstruction of his chosen path confines him
Yes, if he was delayed
Only if police were involved
Confinement means being held within boundaries on all sides, not merely prevented from going one way.
Harris v. Jones: a supervisor repeatedly mocked an employee's stutter, and he was humiliated. The IIED claim failed because:
His distress wasn’t shown to be severe enough
Mocking a disability can never be outrageous conduct
There was no physical contact
The employer was immune
The court found the conduct outrageous, but the plaintiff did not prove severe emotional distress.
Rob walks across his neighbor's lawn without permission, causing no damage. The neighbor sues. Result?
Liable for at least nominal damages
Not liable without some damage
Liable only if he had been warned
Not liable, since lawns are open land
Dougherty v. Stepp: entering land without consent is actionable even without harm.
Herrin v. Sutherland: a hunter fired shots over the plaintiff's land without touching the ground. Trespass?
Yes: the shots invaded the airspace
No: nothing physically touched the ground
No: hunting is privileged
Only if livestock were hurt
Intrusions into the immediate airspace above land can be trespass. Modern law limits this to the zone of actual use.
A nurse kisses a sleeping patient, who never learns of it until later. Battery?
Yes: awareness at the time isn’t required
No: the patient didn’t know it happened
No: the patient wasn’t harmed
Only assault, since there was no fear
Offensive contact is battery even if the victim is asleep. Assault, by contrast, requires apprehension and thus awareness.
Wishnatsky v. Huey: an assistant attorney general briefly pushed a door shut on a man entering his office. Battery?
No: it wouldn’t offend a reasonable sense of dignity
Yes: any unwanted contact, however slight, is battery
Yes: he touched the man through the door
Only if the man fell
Offensiveness is judged objectively. A hypersensitive plaintiff cannot make ordinary contact offensive.
Which tort protects the right to exclusive possession of personal property, for minor interference that causes damage?
Trespass to chattels
Conversion
Trespass to land
Private nuisance
Trespass to chattels covers lesser interference with actual harm. Serious interference is conversion.
Intent for battery is satisfied by:
Purpose or knowledge to a substantial certainty
Careless conduct that creates a risk of some contact
Any voluntary movement
Hostile feelings toward the plaintiff
Intent means purpose or substantial certainty of the result.
Trespass to chattels requires:
Intentional interference causing harm or dispossession
Any touching of another’s property, even with no effect at all
Complete destruction of the property
Intent to steal the property
Minor interference without harm isn’t actionable as trespass to chattels.
Damages for conversion are usually:
The property’s full value when converted
Only the reasonable cost of repairing the property
Nominal damages only
Double the property’s value
Conversion forces a judicial sale to the defendant.
IIED requires:
Outrageous conduct, intent or recklessness, severe distress
Physical contact and resulting bodily injury
Negligent conduct causing some distress, with or without symptoms
A false statement about the plaintiff
Those are the elements of intentional infliction.
Whether a contact is offensive is judged by:
A reasonable sense of personal dignity
The plaintiff’s own sensitivity, however unusual
The defendant’s intent to offend
Whether any injury resulted
Offensiveness is an objective test unless the defendant knows of a special sensitivity.
Under transferred intent, intent can move:
From one person to another, and between certain torts
Only from one person to another
Only between intentional torts and negligence claims
Only between property torts
It applies across persons and among assault, battery, false imprisonment, and trespasses.

No: he didn’t intend any contact with Bo
Yes: any contact from an intentional act is battery
Yes: intent transfers from the fly to Bo

Al swings a stick at Bo, meaning only to scare him by stopping short. He misjudges and hits Bo. Battery?
Yes: intent to frighten transfers to the contact
No: he never intended to touch Bo, so it can’t be battery
No: at most it was an assault
Only if Bo saw the stick coming
Transferred intent works between assault and battery.
Cy points an unloaded gun at Di, who doesn’t know it is unloaded. Assault?
Yes: Di reasonably feared imminent contact
No: the gun couldn’t fire
No: Cy never touched her
Only if Cy said something threatening
Apparent ability to cause contact is enough.
Cy points an unloaded gun at Di, who knows it is unloaded and isn’t worried. Assault?
No: she had no apprehension of contact
Yes: pointing a gun is always assault
Yes: Cy intended to frighten her
Only if others were present
Assault requires reasonable apprehension by the plaintiff.
Ed swings at Fay from behind and misses. She never notices. Assault?
No: she wasn’t aware of the threat
Yes: he intended to hit her, and that intent is enough
Yes: a miss is an assault
Only if he was armed
Assault needs the plaintiff to be aware of the imminent contact.
Gus tells Hal, “Tomorrow I’m going to beat you up.” Hal is frightened. Assault?
No: the threatened contact isn’t imminent
Yes: Hal was genuinely afraid
Yes: threatening words alone are enough for an assault
Only if Gus is larger than Hal
Threats of future harm aren’t assault.
Ho locks Ivy in a room for ten minutes. She is asleep, never learns of it, and isn’t harmed. False imprisonment?
No: she was neither aware of nor harmed by it
Yes: any confinement counts
Yes: Ho intended to confine her, which is all that matters
Only if the door was bolted shut

Ho locks Ivy in a room for ten minutes. She tries the door, realizes she is trapped, and panics. False imprisonment?
Yes: she was knowingly confined
No: ten minutes is too short
No: she wasn’t physically harmed
Only if she screamed for help
Intentional, known confinement for any appreciable time is enough.
A crowd shoves Mo onto Ned’s lawn against his will. Trespass to land?
No: Mo didn’t voluntarily enter
Yes: intent isn’t required for trespass
Yes: he was on Ned’s land
Only if he damaged the lawn
Trespass requires a voluntary, intended entry.
Pat takes Quin’s bike for ten minutes without permission and returns it unharmed. Best claim?
Trespass to chattels, at most
Conversion, for the bike’s full value
Battery
No claim of any kind is possible
Brief interference is trespass to chattels, not conversion.
Pat takes Quin’s bike without permission and sells it to a stranger. Best claim?
Conversion
Trespass to chattels only
Trespass to land
No claim, since Quin can find the buyer
Selling another’s property is a serious interference: conversion.
As a joke, Rob falsely tells Sue her husband was badly hurt in a crash. She suffers severe distress for weeks. IIED?
Yes: outrageous conduct causing severe distress
No: Rob meant it only as a joke, so he lacked any intent
No: there was no physical contact
Only if her husband was in fact hurt
Recklessly causing severe distress through outrageous conduct is IIED.
In a meeting, Rob calls Sue “an idiot.” She is upset for a day. IIED?
No: mere insults aren’t outrageous enough
Yes: insults in front of coworkers are outrageous conduct
Yes: she was upset
Only if Rob is her boss
IIED requires conduct beyond all bounds of decency and severe distress.
Tom spits on Uma’s face. She isn’t physically hurt. Battery?
Yes: the contact is offensive
No: there was no injury
No: spit isn’t a contact
Only if she saw it coming
Offensive contact is enough for battery.
Tom spits at Uma, misses, and she never notices. Battery or assault?
Neither
Battery
Assault
Both
No contact and no apprehension means neither tort.
A seller says a house has no termites, knowing it does. The buyer relies on that and buys. Best tort claim?
Fraudulent misrepresentation
Negligent misrepresentation only
Defamation
No claim, since the buyer could inspect
Knowing falsity, intent to induce reliance, and justifiable reliance make fraud.
A seller honestly and reasonably believes a house has no termites and says so. It does have them. Fraudulent misrepresentation?
No: the seller didn’t know it was false
Yes: the statement was false
Yes: the buyer relied on the statement in deciding to buy
Only if the buyer is a business
Fraud requires scienter: knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard.
Val, knowing Wes has an exclusive deal with Xi, persuades Wes to break it so Val can hire him. Best claim for Xi against Val?
Interference with contractual relations
Conversion of Wes’s services
Defamation of Xi’s business
No claim against Val; only Wes, who broke the deal, is liable
Knowingly inducing a breach of another’s agreement is interference.
A dry cleaner accidentally ruins a customer’s coat beyond repair. Conversion?
No: conversion needs an intent to exercise control
Yes: the coat was destroyed
Yes: the cleaner had possession
Only if the coat was expensive
Accidental damage is negligence, not conversion.
A masked man shows a knife and says, “Hand over your wallet or I’ll stab you right now.” Assault?
Yes: the threat is imminent despite the condition
No: he gave her a choice
No: words alone can’t be assault
Only if he moves toward her
A conditional threat the defendant has no right to impose is still assault.
A guard tells a visitor, “If you leave this room, I’ll shoot you.” She stays. False imprisonment?
Yes: confinement by threat of force
No: the door wasn’t locked
No: she chose to stay
Only if he had a gun visible
Threats of force can confine.
A man learns by phone days later that his mother was brutally beaten. Can he sue the attacker for IIED as a bystander?
Unlikely: he wasn’t present
Yes: he is immediate family
Yes: the conduct was outrageous
Only if he was physically hurt
Third-party IIED usually requires presence.
Ty intentionally throws a ball onto his neighbor’s yard to annoy her. Trespass to land?
Yes: intentionally causing an object to enter counts
No: Ty never entered
No: there was no damage
Only if she asked him to stop
Causing a thing to enter land is a trespass.

topics.name: Tort Defenses & Immunities
terms: Consent
Willingness in fact for conduct to occur, shown by words or conduct.
Implied consent
Consent inferred from conduct, custom or circumstances.
Emergency exception
Consent implied for urgent treatment when a patient cannot consent and delay risks serious harm.
Self-defense
Privilege to use reasonable force one reasonably believes necessary to prevent imminent harmful contact.
Defense of others
Privilege to use reasonable force to protect a third person from attack.
Defense of property
Privilege to use reasonable, non-deadly force to prevent or end an intrusion on one’s land or chattels.
Recapture of chattels
Privilege to use reasonable force in fresh pursuit to regain wrongfully taken property.
Shopkeeper’s privilege
A merchant’s right to detain a suspected shoplifter reasonably, briefly and on reasonable belief.
Public necessity
Complete privilege to damage property to avert an imminent disaster to the community.
Private necessity
Incomplete privilege to use another’s property to prevent greater harm to oneself, paying for damage.
Contributory negligence
A plaintiff’s own carelessness, which at common law completely barred recovery.
Last clear chance
Doctrine letting a negligent plaintiff recover if the defendant had the final opportunity to avoid harm.
Pure comparative fault
Recovery reduced by the plaintiff’s percentage of fault, however large.
Modified comparative fault
Reduced recovery allowed only if the plaintiff’s fault stays below a 50% or 51% threshold.
Express assumption of risk
An explicit agreement, like a signed waiver, releasing the defendant from liability.
Primary assumption of risk
A no-duty rule for risks inherent in an activity the plaintiff chose.
Secondary assumption of risk
Knowingly encountering a risk created by the defendant’s negligence, now usually part of comparative fault.
Exculpatory clause
A contract term releasing a party from liability for its own negligence.
Statute of limitations
A deadline for filing suit, measured from when the claim accrues.
Discovery rule
Starts the limitations clock when the plaintiff knew or should have known of the injury and its cause.
Statute of repose
A fixed filing deadline measured from an event, such as a product’s sale, regardless of injury.
Sovereign immunity
Government immunity from suit unless it consents.
Federal Tort Claims Act
Federal statute waiving U.S. immunity for many negligence claims, with exceptions.
Discretionary function exception
FTCA bar on claims based on government policy judgments.
Feres doctrine
Bar on FTCA claims by service members for injuries incident to military service.
Charitable immunity
A former rule shielding charities from tort liability, now largely abolished.
Intrafamily immunity
A former bar on suits between spouses or between parents and children.
cases: Mohr v. Williams
Operating on a different ear than the one consented to was a battery.
O’Brien v. Cunard
Holding up an arm in a vaccination line manifested consent.
Hudson v. Craft
Consent to an illegal prize fight did not bar a fighter the statute protected.
Katko v. Briney
A spring gun protecting an empty farmhouse was unprivileged deadly force.
Courvoisier v. Raymond
Self-defense covers reasonable but mistaken belief in a threat.
Vincent v. Lake Erie
A ship kept moored in a storm under private necessity had to pay for dock damage.
Ploof v. Putnam
A dock owner could not unmoor a boat seeking shelter from a storm under necessity.
Surocco v. Geary
Destroying a house to stop a citywide fire was privileged public necessity.
Coblyn v. Kennedy’s
Detaining an elderly shopper without reasonable grounds exceeded the shopkeeper’s privilege.
Butterfield v. Forrester
A plaintiff’s own lack of ordinary care barred recovery.
Li v. Yellow Cab
California replaced contributory negligence with pure comparative fault.
Murphy v. Steeplechase Amusement
A rider accepted the obvious risks of a ride designed to make people fall.
Tunkl v. Regents
A hospital’s release of negligence liability violated public policy.
Knight v. Jewett
Sports coparticipants owe no duty to avoid ordinary carelessness inherent in the game.
mcq: A store detains a suspected shoplifter for 20 minutes, reasonably and on a reasonable belief. She turns out to be innocent. Is the store liable for false imprisonment?
No: the shopkeeper's privilege applies
Yes: liability is strict once she is innocent
Yes: any detention without a warrant is unlawful
No: there was no physical barrier
The shopkeeper's privilege covers a detention on reasonable belief, in a reasonable manner, for a reasonable time.
During a storm a ship stays moored to a dock and damages it (Vincent v. Lake Erie). Is the shipowner liable?
Yes: private necessity still requires paying for damage
No: necessity is a complete defense, so it owes nothing
No: storm damage is an act of God
Yes, including punitive damages
Private necessity lets the ship stay moored, but the owner must still pay for the damage it causes.
A patient consents to surgery on her right ear. The surgeon operates on the left ear instead, with no emergency. Battery?
Yes: the surgeon went beyond the consent given
No: the surgery was beneficial
No: consent to surgery covers related procedures
Only if the operation failed
Mohr v. Williams: acting outside the scope of consent is a battery even if skillful and in good faith.
Officials destroy a house to stop a fire from spreading across the city. Can the owner recover from them in tort?
No: public necessity is a complete privilege
Yes: private necessity requires payment
Yes: destruction of property is always compensable
Only if the fire never reached the house
Surocco v. Geary: public necessity is complete. Any compensation comes from statute or takings law.
Under traditional contributory negligence, a plaintiff who is 5% at fault recovers:
Nothing, unless last clear chance applies
95% of damages, reduced by her share
50% of damages, as a split
Full damages, since the defendant was worse
Contributory negligence was a complete bar, softened by last clear chance.
A plaintiff is 60% at fault and has $100,000 in damages. Under pure comparative negligence she recovers:
Pure comparative fault reduces recovery by the plaintiff's share. Under a modified 50% or 51% bar she would get nothing.
A plaintiff is 40% at fault with $100,000 in damages, in a modified comparative fault state with a 50% bar. She recovers:
Below the threshold, recovery is reduced by her share. At or above it (depending on the state's version), she recovers nothing.
A fan at a baseball game is hit by a foul ball in the stands. Typical result?
No recovery: primary assumption of an inherent risk
Full recovery: the stadium is strictly liable
Recovery reduced by comparative fault
Recovery only if the stadium had no netting anywhere
Primary assumption of risk means no duty to protect against risks inherent in the activity.
A hospital requires every patient to sign a release of all negligence claims before treatment. Is it enforceable?
No: releases for essential public services are void
Yes: the patient signed it voluntarily and knowingly
Yes, if the release was printed in bold
Only for minor injuries during treatment
Tunkl v. Regents: exculpatory clauses are unenforceable where the service is essential and bargaining power unequal.
O'Brien v. Cunard: a passenger held up her arm in a line of people receiving vaccinations. Consent?
Yes: her conduct showed consent
No: consent must be given in words, not gestures
No: she was under duress
Only if she signed a form
Consent can be implied from conduct. The surgeon reasonably relied on her apparent willingness.
Courvoisier v. Raymond: a shopkeeper shot a man he reasonably but mistakenly believed was attacking him. Privilege?
Yes: self-defense covers reasonable mistakes
No: the man was innocent, so he’s liable
No: deadly force is never privileged
Only if the man was armed
Self-defense turns on what the defendant reasonably believed, not on the actual facts.
A homeowner sees a trespasser walking across her lawn. Before using any force to remove him, she generally must:
Ask him to leave, unless that’s futile or dangerous
Call the police before doing anything
Post a sign warning him to stay off
Nothing; reasonable force is always allowed right away
Defense of property requires a request to leave first unless it would be useless, and force must be reasonable and non-deadly.
Knight v. Jewett: a woman was hurt in a casual touch football game. Coparticipants in sports are liable only for:
Intentional injury or reckless conduct
Any careless play during the game
All contact, since football is risky
Nothing at all
Primary assumption of risk: no duty to avoid ordinary carelessness inherent in the sport.
Li v. Yellow Cab is known for:
Adopting pure comparative negligence in California
Creating the attractive nuisance doctrine for child trespassers
Abolishing strict products liability
Recognizing the tort of IIED
California replaced contributory negligence with pure comparative fault.
Murphy v. Steeplechase Amusement: a man was hurt on 'The Flopper,' a ride designed to make people fall. Cardozo held:
No recovery: he accepted an obvious risk
The park was strictly liable
Comparative fault split the loss
The ride was an attractive nuisance
Volunteers accept the obvious, inherent dangers of a sport or amusement.
Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a claim attacking an agency's policy decision about how to allocate safety funding is barred by the:
Discretionary function rule
Feres doctrine for service members
Statute of repose
Firefighter’s rule
The FTCA waives immunity for ordinary negligence but bars claims based on policy judgments.
A surgeon leaves a sponge in a patient, who discovers it seven years later. The limitations period is two years. In most states:
The discovery rule starts the clock when she knew or should have known
The claim is barred, since seven years have passed since the surgery took place
There is no limitations period for medical claims
She must sue within 30 days of discovery
The discovery rule delays accrual until the plaintiff knew or reasonably should have known of the injury and its cause.
Under the Feres doctrine, a service member injured by military doctors' negligence during service generally:
Cannot sue the United States under the FTCA
Can sue like any civilian
Can sue the military doctors personally for malpractice
Can sue only for intentional misconduct
Feres bars FTCA claims for injuries incident to military service.
Charitable and intrafamily immunities today are best described as:
Largely abolished or narrowed
Expanding in most states
Absolute in most states
Limited to intentional torts
Most states have eliminated charitable immunity and narrowed parent-child and spousal immunity.
Deadly force in self-defense is allowed when the actor reasonably believes she faces:
Death or serious bodily harm
Any offensive contact
A threat to her property
An insult

Under “last clear chance,” a contributorily negligent plaintiff could still recover if:
The defendant had the final chance to avoid harm
The plaintiff was less careless than the defendant
The defendant was insured against the loss
The plaintiff apologized for her carelessness
Last clear chance softened the contributory negligence bar.
Primary implied assumption of risk means:
The defendant had no duty as to inherent risks
The plaintiff’s own fault reduces her damages proportionally
The plaintiff signed a release
The defendant acted intentionally
It reflects a no-duty rule for risks inherent in an activity.
Defense of property generally permits:
Reasonable non-deadly force, usually after a request
Any force needed to protect property
Deadly force against any trespasser who refuses to leave
Force only after calling the police
Force must be reasonable and usually preceded by a request.
A statute of repose differs from a statute of limitations because it:
Runs from a fixed event regardless of discovery
Runs from the plaintiff’s discovery of harm
Applies only to intentional torts
Can be waived by the court
Repose periods cut off claims even before discovery.
A reasonable mistake about the need for self-defense:
Doesn’t defeat the privilege
Defeats the privilege
Makes the defender strictly liable
Shifts liability to the police
Courvoisier: the privilege covers reasonable mistakes.

No: it was far more than needed
Yes: he struck first
